title: If We Don't Build Boyhood Spaces, the Internet Will
author: Ned Erickson
summary: Prompted by a leaked memo suggesting the Pentagon may sever its ties with Scouting America over the question of 'boy-friendly spaces,' this Fatherhood Framework essay uses the news hook to make a developmental argument: boys still need structured, mentored spaces built for them, and when those spaces disappear something else fills the vacuum. The author is careful to distinguish the claim from nostalgia, exclusion, or a wish to return to 1954 — it is about how boys actually learn, test themselves, and mature. Pairing this with a prior piece on what young men need to subtract (porn, social media, video games, the smartphone dopamine drip), he argues subtraction is only half the equation and that boys need real, embodied spaces added back in: places to take risks, struggle, fail, and try again under the guidance of older men modeling strength without aggression and confidence without arrogance. The essay's engine is a substitution logic — remove real mentors, challenges, and community and boys turn to digital mentors, artificial challenges, and online tribes, because the algorithm never waits and does not care about their well-being. He grants that flawed institutions needed reform but warns that we stripped the scaffolding without replacing it, and concludes that if adults don't give boys somewhere better to go, the screen will raise them, and raise them badly.
points: The argument is developmental, not nostalgic: 'boy-friendly spaces' are defended as structured environments where boys take risks, fail, and are guided by older men — explicitly not about exclusion, supremacy, or turning back the clock.
Subtraction is only half the equation — removing porn, social media, gaming, and smartphone dependence must be paired with adding back real, embodied, mentored spaces, or the vacuum simply refills.

The essay's core mechanism is substitution: take away real mentors and boys find digital ones, take away real challenges and they chase artificial ones, take away real community and they latch onto whatever online tribe offers the clearest identity.

Male-centered spaces are framed as 'shock absorbers' that teach boys to channel aggression into discipline and energy into purpose, and to distinguish confidence from cruelty and strength from dominance.

The wider institutional point is that the specific vehicle (Scouts, the Pentagon partnership) is negotiable but the underlying need is not — boys will learn to be men somewhere, and the only question is whether that happens in the real world or through a screen.
quotes: But subtraction is only half the equation. You also have to add something.
Boys need environments that challenge them and give them direction. They need chances to take risks, struggle, fail, and try again.

Take away real mentors, and boys find digital ones. Take away real challenges, and boys chase artificial ones. Take away real community, and boys latch onto whatever online tribe offers the clearest identity.
Male-centered spaces - healthy, structured, guided spaces - aren’t luxuries. They’re shock absorbers.
Boys don’t become good men accidentally. They need structure, they need guidance, and they need adults who are capable of exhibiting responsible masculinity.
Because if we don’t, the screen will raise them for us. And it won’t raise them well.
